calculators.title: Pediatric Appendicitis Score

bands.text: 3 or less: below ACR's equivocal band
8 or more: above the equivocal band; ultrasound first in a child

sources.where: Clinical Decision Tools for Pediatric Appendicitis

calculators.note: Cut points differ: ACR's staged pathway (citing Saucier) images an equivocal 4 to 7, the Dutch review rules appendicitis out at 5 or less, and StatPearls reads 6 or more as suggestive. WSES advises against making the diagnosis on a score alone.

nodes.ask: Vomiting child in the ED. First moves?
options: Weigh the child; check the airway, perfusion and a fingerstick glucose
Blood count, electrolytes and a venous gas to grade the dehydration
Oral ondansetron first, then a full assessment once the vomiting settles
Abdominal x-ray to exclude obstruction before fluid is started
nodes.chainStep: Weigh the child (every fluid and dose is per kg); airway and breathing; perfusion: level of consciousness, skin color, warmth of the hands and feet, pulses, capillary refill, heart rate, blood pressure; fingerstick glucose, with blood ketones and a venous gas if it is high
nodes.why: Fluids and drugs in a child are calculated from body weight, so the weight comes first. Shock is a bedside diagnosis: decreased consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, weak pulses, prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia and, late, hypotension. A stick glucose under 60 mg/dL is treated at once (AES; WHO's chart uses 2.5 mmol/L, 45 mg/dL, in a well-nourished child), and a high one is checked for ketoacidosis. Blood tests are not routine in gastroenteritis; they are for the child who needs IV fluid or may be hypernatremic. A film comes only once obstruction is suspected, and an antiemetic is a question for later, once shock and the red flags are excluded.

orders.dose: Body weight is used to calculate IV fluid and electrolyte needs

One or more expected: decreased consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, tachycardia, tachypnea, weak peripheral pulses, prolonged capillary refill; hypotension means decompensated shock

AES 2016: under 60 mg/dL in a child; 25% dextrose 2 mL/kg from 2 years, 12.5% dextrose 4 mL/kg under 2. WHO: under 2.5 mmol/L (45 mg/dL) if well nourished, under 3 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) if severely malnourished
orders.note: WHO's triage chart treats at a lower glucose; this pathway treats under 60 mg/dL, as pw_peds_fever and pw_seizure do.

orders.dose: DKA needs all three: glucose over 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL), venous pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 18 mmol/L, and ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate 3 mmol/L or more) or moderate or large ketonuria

nodes.note: Not in this version: the newborn in the first 2 days of life (ACR images with a radiograph first), necrotizing enterocolitis, reflux disease beyond the well infant, metabolic and endocrine causes such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, eosinophilic disease, pregnancy, and the adolescent with cannabis hyperemesis.

nodes.label: Perfusion, the fingerstick glucose and ketones

outcomes.if: Diabetic ketoacidosis picture; high glucose with ketones and acidosis, shocked or not
Shocked, no ketoacidosis; cold or mottled, weak pulses, slow refill
Low glucose, perfused; under 60 mg/dL on the stick test
Perfused, glucose 60 mg/dL or more; no shock sign, no ketoacidosis

nodes.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis in a child: pw_dka_hhs walks the crisis for adults, and a child follows ISPAD 2022 instead. Fluid comes before insulin: 0.9% saline 10 to 20 mL/kg over 20 to 30 minutes to restore the circulation, or 20 mL/kg boluses as quickly as possible in the rare child in shock, then the deficit replaced over 24 to 48 hours. Insulin runs at 0.05 to 0.1 U/kg/h, started at least 1 hour after the fluid, with no IV insulin bolus. Headache or vomiting after treatment starts, a slowing heart rate or a change in neurological state are warning signs of cerebral injury.

options: Glucose-free isotonic crystalloid bolus by weight, then reassess
5% dextrose bolus by weight, treating the shock and glucose together
Hydroxyethyl starch bolus by weight, as it stays in the vessels
IV ondansetron and an oral fluid trial before starting IV fluid
nodes.chainStep: 0.9% saline, or another glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L, as a rapid bolus by weight (NICE 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes; WHO and StatPearls 20 mL/kg); reassess after each; if still shocked a second bolus and a search for other causes; PICU advice if still shocked after the second, and expert advice at 40 to 60 mL/kg; venous gas with chloride, and sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose
nodes.why: Shock gets a rapid IV bolus of a glucose-free isotonic crystalloid, with a reassessment after each one. NICE gives 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline over less than 10 minutes, repeats it once, considers other causes of shock, and calls the paediatric intensive care team if the child stays shocked; WHO and StatPearls give 20 mL/kg. Glucose solutions are not resuscitation fluids: 5% glucose risks hyponatremia and cerebral edema, and a low glucose is treated on its own with 10% glucose. Tetrastarch is not used. An antiemetic and an oral trial belong to the child who is not shocked.

orders.dose: NICE: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline over less than 10 minutes, repeated once if still shocked. WHO: 20 mL/kg of Ringer's lactate or saline as rapidly as possible, then 10 to 20 mL/kg if no improvement. StatPearls: 20 mL/kg of saline within 20 minutes, repeated on reassessment
orders.note: NICE CG84 and NG29 give half the 20 mL/kg bolus that WHO, StatPearls and ISPAD (for DKA in shock) use; US practice uses 20 mL/kg.

orders.dose: A second rapid bolus and other causes of shock considered; paediatric intensive care advice if still shocked after the second; expert advice if 40 to 60 mL/kg or more is needed
Not for fluid resuscitation
Not for rehydration: they raise the risk of hyponatremia and cerebral edema
10% glucose 5 mL/kg IV, rechecked at 30 minutes
Venous acid-base status and chloride; sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose once IV fluid is needed

outcomes.if: Shock resolves; alert, warm, pulses and refill back
Still shocked, surgical abdomen; green vomit, distension, peritonitis or rectal blood
Still shocked, abdomen soft; after two boluses, no surgical sign

nodes.summary: Shock with a surgical abdomen: resuscitation continues on the way to theatre. In an infant with bilious vomiting, peritonitis, sepsis or instability means the operating room without waiting for complete imaging, with the airway protected, nasogastric or orogastric decompression, IV fluid and broad-spectrum antibiotics, because midgut volvulus can progress to transmural necrosis within hours. Peritonitis, free air or shock also rule out enema reduction of an intussusception, which is treated surgically.

Still shocked after two boluses with a soft abdomen: NICE consults the paediatric intensive care team, considers causes of shock other than dehydration and gives antibiotics to any child with suspected or confirmed septicaemia (CG84 1.5.1.2); WHO repeats 20 mL/kg when profuse diarrhea is the cause. Septic shock in a child continues in pw_peds_fever.

nodes.ask: Perfused child, glucose under 60 mg/dL, IV line in. Next?
options: 10% glucose 5 mL/kg IV now, recheck in 30 minutes, then feed
50% dextrose 1 mL/kg pushed through the hand vein, then recheck
5% dextrose at the maintenance rate, with a recheck in 4 hours
0.9% saline 20 mL/kg first, then glucose once rehydrated
nodes.chainStep: 10% glucose 5 mL/kg IV (0.5 g/kg); recheck in 30 minutes and repeat 5 mL/kg if still low; feed once awake, or run IV fluid containing 5 to 10% glucose; then look for the cause
nodes.why: With a line in, a low glucose is corrected at once with IV glucose. WHO gives 5 mL/kg of 10% glucose rapidly, rechecks at 30 minutes and repeats it if still low, then feeds the child or runs fluid containing 5 to 10% glucose. StatPearls gives 0.5 to 1 g/kg, as 5 to 10 mL/kg of 10% dextrose or 2 to 4 mL/kg of 25%, and keeps 50% dextrose for an adolescent with a large-bore line. A maintenance drip is too slow, and a saline bolus first leaves the low glucose untreated.

orders.dose: 10% glucose 5 mL/kg rapidly IV; recheck at 30 minutes and repeat 5 mL/kg if still low; feed once conscious, or IV fluid containing 5 to 10% glucose
0.5 to 1 g/kg: 5 to 10 mL/kg of 10% dextrose or 2 to 4 mL/kg of 25%; 1 to 2 mL/kg of 50% only in an adolescent with a large-bore line
Which samples to draw before the glucose (insulin, cortisol, ketones) is not in the sources read

nodes.ask: Perfused, glucose safe. What decides the route?
options: Red flags: bile, blood, head injury, pain site, testes, rash, toxins
A blood count and CRP, to separate a viral cause from a bacterial one
A plain abdominal film first, then the history and examination
An oral fluid challenge first, examining if it comes back up
nodes.chainStep: History and examination for features of another diagnosis (NICE): green vomit, blood or mucus in the stool, severe or localized pain, distension or rebound, head injury or raised pressure signs, altered consciousness, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, a non-blanching rash, fever (38 or more under 3 months, 39 or more from 3 months); testes and groin; possible ingestions; then the age, the vomit and the stools
nodes.why: NICE lists the features that point away from gastroenteritis: fever of 38 or more under 3 months or 39 or more from 3 months, breathlessness, altered consciousness, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, a non-blanching rash, blood or mucus in the stool, bilious (green) vomit, severe or localized pain, and distension or rebound. ACR evaluates bilious or repeated forceful vomiting for obstruction. Testicular and ovarian torsion can both present with vomiting. A blood count does not sort the causes, and a film or an oral trial before the examination delays the surgical diagnoses.

nodes.label: Red flags on history and examination

outcomes.if: Green vomit, no colicky attacks; bilious, most often an infant
Colicky attacks with pallor; legs drawn up, quiet between, under 3 years
Right lower quadrant pain, not sudden; pain came before the vomiting
Testis pain, or sudden pelvic pain; a painful testis or groin, or a girl with sudden one-sided pelvic pain
Head injury or raised pressure, no fever; after a knock, or morning headache

lead: Head injury or raised intracranial pressure

orders.dose: GCS 14 to 15 after injury. Aged 2 or younger: CT for a GCS of 14 or less, a palpable skull fracture or altered mental status; CT or observation for loss of consciousness of 5 seconds or more, a severe mechanism, an occipital, parietal or temporal scalp hematoma, or not acting normally. Aged 2 or older: CT for a GCS of 14 or less, basilar skull fracture signs or altered mental status; CT or observation for loss of consciousness, severe headache, vomiting or a severe mechanism. Otherwise no CT

sources.where: 1.5.10; 1.5.11; 1.5.12; Rationale: criteria for doing a CT head scan

orders.note: NICE counts 3 or more vomits as one of two risk factors needed for CT and observes for one; PECARN puts any vomiting in CT or observation. NICE NG232 found the rules not very different, PECARN vaguer and without timings. StatPearls words the PECARN age bands as 2 or younger and 2 or older.

outcomes.if: Possible ingestion; tablets, a button battery or a household product
Fever red flag, no surgical sign; 38 or more under 3 months, 39 or more from 3 months, a non-blanching rash, stiff neck or bulging fontanelle
Bloody diarrhea, vomit not green; loose stools with blood, no colicky attacks
No red flag; non-bilious vomit, soft abdomen, no blood

nodes.summary: Torsion is a surgical emergency, and vomiting is part of both. A painful testis or groin: pw_scrotal_pain takes it from here (its TWIST score gives a point for nausea or vomiting). A girl with sudden one-sided pelvic pain: pelvic ultrasound with Doppler, the imaging study of choice, and pw_abdominal_pain takes it from there with emergency surgery whatever the Doppler flow shows.

Head injury or raised pressure. After a head injury in a child, NICE does a CT head within 1 hour for suspected non-accidental injury, a post-traumatic seizure, a GCS under 14 in the ED (under 15 in a baby under 1), a GCS under 15 at 2 hours, a suspected open or depressed fracture or tense fontanelle, a sign of basal skull fracture, a focal deficit, or in a baby under 1 a head bruise, swelling or cut over 5 cm; and for more than one of: witnessed loss of consciousness over 5 minutes, abnormal drowsiness, 3 or more discrete vomits, a dangerous mechanism, amnesia over 5 minutes, a bleeding or clotting disorder. With only one of those the child is observed for at least 4 hours from the injury, and a GCS under 15, further vomiting or more drowsiness means CT within 1 hour. Without an injury, vomiting with headache, altered mental status, papilledema or a bulging fontanelle raises intracranial hypertension: CT or MRI, the head of the bed at about 30 degrees, and osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline (StatPearls: mannitol 0.25 to 1 g/kg; its pediatric head trauma chapter calls mannitol potentially detrimental after pediatric TBI). pw_trauma and pw_headache are written for adults.

Possible ingestion: pw_tox takes the poisoning workup from here, though it is written for adults and leaves out caustics. A suspected button battery gets AP and lateral films of the head, neck, chest and abdomen at once. A low-risk child without symptoms whose battery has passed the esophagus is followed with films at 10 to 14 days (at 4 days if under 6 or the battery is 15 mm or more), with early endoscopy considered under 5 years or for a battery over 20 mm; every other child has emergent endoscopic removal.

Fever with a red flag (38 or more under 3 months, 39 or more from 3 months, a non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, altered consciousness) points away from gastroenteritis (NICE) and toward sepsis or meningitis: pw_peds_fever takes it from here, and pw_rash carries the non-blanching rash workup.

nodes.label: Age, the vomiting and the stools

outcomes.if: Projectile, 2 weeks to 3 months; non-bilious, hungry after, no diarrhea
Acute vomiting or diarrhea; not a projectile young infant, no past attacks
Stereotyped attacks, well between; 4 or more in a year, a week apart
Well infant, effortless spit-ups; gaining weight, not projectile

nodes.summary: Cyclic vomiting syndrome in a child (Rome V and NASPGHAN 2025, as summarized in StatPearls): stereotyped episodes of vomiting several times an hour, at least 4 in 12 months, each lasting 2 hours to 7 days, at least a week apart, a return to baseline between, and other causes excluded; screening bloods, urinalysis and an upper GI series to exclude malrotation. An attack is treated with IV fluid containing dextrose, IV antiemetics (ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg, at most 8 mg a dose) and a quiet, dark room. Prophylaxis is for episodes more than 4 times a year, longer than 2 days, or needing the ED.

Not pyloric stenosis. A well infant with effortless spit-ups who is otherwise healthy has reflux, and imaging is usually not necessary (ACR). A normal pyloric ultrasound in an infant who keeps vomiting may be pylorospasm, treated conservatively, but its measurements overlap with evolving pyloric stenosis, so ACR advises careful follow-up and repeat imaging over time. Green vomit or poor weight gain sends the infant back to the red flags.

nodes.ask: Gastroenteritis picture, perfused. How dry is the child?
options: Grade it from the clinical signs; bloods only if IV fluid is needed
Grade it from a serum bicarbonate and urea sent at triage
Grade it from the urine specific gravity and urine ketones
Grade it from the number of stools and vomits over the past 24 hours
nodes.chainStep: Grade dehydration at the bedside (NICE table 1, or the WHO signs): responsiveness, eyes, mucous membranes, heart and breathing rate, pulses, capillary refill, skin turgor, urine output; no routine bloods; sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose if IV fluid is needed or hypernatremia is suspected; stool culture for blood or mucus, septicemia or immunocompromise
nodes.why: Dehydration is graded from the clinical signs. NICE separates no clinically detectable dehydration, clinical dehydration (its red flags: appears unwell, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnea, reduced skin turgor) and shock; WHO calls it some or severe dehydration on two or more signs. NICE does not routinely send blood tests: they are for a child who needs IV fluid or may be hypernatremic. StatPearls notes that no proven tool determines the degree of dehydration in children; urine ketones only suggest it is more severe, and the stool and vomit counts are NICE risk factors, not a grade.

orders.dose: Appears unwell or deteriorating, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnea, reduced skin turgor

Some dehydration: two or more of restless or irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly. Severe: two or more of lethargy, sunken eyes, drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (2 seconds or more)
Not routine; sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose if IV fluid is needed or hypernatremia is suggested (jittery movements, increased tone, hyperreflexia, convulsions, drowsiness)
Under 1 year (above all under 6 months), low birth weight, more than 5 stools or more than 2 vomits in 24 hours, stopped breastfeeding, signs of malnutrition
With blood or mucus, suspected septicemia or immunocompromise; consider after travel, diarrhea past day 7 or an uncertain diagnosis

outcomes.if: No clinical dehydration; alert, moist mouth, eyes normal, passing urine
Clinical dehydration, not lethargic; dry mouth, less urine, perfused
Severe dehydration, not shocked; lethargic, drinks poorly, skin pinch 2 seconds or more

orders.dose: NICE: ORS unless shock, deterioration despite ORS or persistent vomiting. WHO plan C: 100 mL/kg IV
orders.note: NICE has no severe grade short of shock; WHO rehydrates severe dehydration IV.

outcomes.if: Shock treated with boluses; perfusion now restored

nodes.ask: Clinical dehydration, never shocked. Rehydrate how?
options: Low-osmolarity ORS by weight over 4 hours, in small, frequent sips
IV 0.9% saline over 4 hours, since the child is still vomiting
Diluted apple juice or a sports drink, whichever the child prefers
Loperamide to cut the losses, then ORS in small frequent sips
nodes.chainStep: Low-osmolarity ORS (240 to 250 mOsm/L) in small amounts often (5 mL every 1 to 2 minutes): NICE 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, WHO 75 mL/kg over 4 hours; breastfeeding continues; nasogastric ORS if the child cannot drink it or vomits persistently; regular reassessment
nodes.why: Oral rehydration solution treats clinical dehydration, hypernatremic dehydration included, unless IV fluid is indicated: shock, deterioration with red flags despite oral rehydration, or persistent vomiting of the ORS by mouth or tube (NICE). It is given frequently in small amounts; StatPearls notes 5 mL every 1 to 2 minutes is usually tolerated. Juice and fizzy drinks are discouraged, high-sugar drinks may worsen diarrhea, and antidiarrheal drugs are not used.

orders.dose: NICE: 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance. WHO plan B: about 75 mL/kg over 4 hours. StatPearls: 50 to 100 mL/kg over 3 to 4 hours
orders.note: The same oral route with different deficit volumes; NICE adds maintenance on top.

orders.dose: Low-osmolarity ORS, 240 to 250 mOsm/L, given frequently in small amounts
If the child cannot drink it or vomits persistently

orders.item: Fruit juice, fizzy drinks, sports drinks
orders.dose: Discouraged; high-sugar drinks may worsen diarrhea
Not used
Not routine in gastroenteritis

outcomes.if: Taking the ORS; vomiting settles, passing urine
Vomits the ORS, 8 kg or more; most sips come back, no worse
Vomits the ORS, under 8 kg; most sips come back, no worse
Deteriorating despite ORS; more lethargic, faster pulse, red flags

nodes.ask: Vomiting stops the ORS; 8 kg or more, perfused. Next?
options: One oral ondansetron dose by weight, then ORS again in small sips
Oral metoclopramide dose by weight, then ORS again in small sips
A 4 hour pause in drinking to settle the gut, then clear fluids
A rectal promethazine dose by weight, then ORS again in small sips
nodes.chainStep: Ondansetron by mouth once (Drugs Context review: 2 mg at 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg over 15 to 30 kg, 8 mg over 30 kg; may be repeated if vomited within 15 minutes), then ORS again in small amounts; nasogastric ORS if it still fails (NICE); not with a prolonged QT
nodes.why: A single oral ondansetron dose makes oral rehydration more likely to work and cuts IV fluid and admission (Drugs Context review); in a primary care trial in children 6 months to 6 years, 0.1 mg/kg cut continued vomiting at 4 hours from 42.9% to 19.5%. Metoclopramide, promethazine, domperidone and the other antiemetics are not recommended in children, for lack of efficacy data or for adverse events. Withholding fluid does not rehydrate; after a vomit the WHO plan waits 10 minutes, then gives ORS more slowly. The sources disagree on antiemetics: WHO advises against them in young children with diarrhea, and NICE CG84 does not address them.

orders.dose: One oral dose by weight band: 2 mg at 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg over 15 to 30 kg, 8 mg over 30 kg, may be repeated if vomited within 15 minutes (Drugs Context review); the primary care trial gave 0.1 mg/kg to children 6 months to 6 years
orders.note: WHO says anti-emetics should not be given to young children with diarrhea; NICE CG84 is silent; the review, StatPearls and the trial support a single dose, as US practice does.

orders.dose: The IDSA 2017 age limit could not be read (its copy is blocked); the open trial enrolled from 6 months
Avoid ondansetron with a prolonged QT interval; ECG and electrolytes when there are arrhythmia risk factors
Metoclopramide, promethazine, domperidone, prochlorperazine and the rest: not recommended in children

orders.item: If the ORS still comes back
orders.dose: Nasogastric ORS; IV fluid if it is vomited by mouth or by tube

outcomes.if: Keeps the ORS down; rehydrating, passing urine
Still vomiting the ORS; by mouth or by nasogastric tube

nodes.ask: IV rehydration is now needed. Fluid and volume?
options: Isotonic fluid for the deficit plus maintenance, electrolytes checked
0.45% saline with 5% glucose for both the deficit and the maintenance
Maintenance fluid without a deficit, so it is not over-corrected
5% glucose in water to replace the whole deficit over 24 hours
nodes.chainStep: 0.9% saline, or 0.9% saline with 5% glucose: deficit 100 mL/kg after shock boluses or 50 mL/kg without, added to maintenance (Holliday-Segar: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10, 20 above 20 kg); sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose at the start and regularly; potassium once the level is known and the child is passing urine; ORS reintroduced early and IV stopped once tolerated
nodes.why: NICE rehydrates IV with an isotonic solution, 0.9% saline or 0.9% saline with 5% glucose, adding a deficit of 100 mL/kg after shock boluses, or 50 mL/kg without shock, to maintenance, with electrolytes and glucose measured at the outset and potassium considered once the level is known. NG29 also uses isotonic fluid for maintenance. Hypotonic and glucose-only fluids risk hyponatremia, and WHO does not use 5% glucose or 0.18% saline with 5% dextrose to rehydrate. Maintenance alone leaves the deficit in place. Oral rehydration comes back as soon as it is tolerated.

orders.dose: Add 100 mL/kg after shock boluses, or 50 mL/kg if not shocked, to maintenance, and monitor the response
100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg, 20 mL/kg/day above 20 kg
0.9% saline, or 0.9% saline with 5% glucose; isotonic crystalloid with sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L for maintenance
100 mL/kg of Ringer's lactate or saline: under 12 months 30 mL/kg in 1 hour then 70 mL/kg in 5 hours; 12 months and older 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg in 2.5 hours
orders.note: WHO gives the 100 mL/kg in 3 to 6 hours; NICE adds the same deficit to maintenance and sets no time.

orders.dose: Consider IV potassium once the plasma level is known; confirm the child is passing urine first
Urgent expert advice; isotonic fluid; the deficit replaced over about 48 hours with sodium falling less than 0.5 mmol/L an hour (NG29: no more than 12 mmol/L in 24 hours)
Early and gradual during IV fluid; IV stopped once the ORS is tolerated

nodes.summary: Under 8 kg and vomiting the ORS: nasogastric ORS (NICE), and IV fluid if it is vomited by mouth or by tube. The review's ondansetron bands start at 8 kg and the trial enrolled from 6 months, so no dose is given here.

Home care: breastfeeding and milk feeds continue, full-strength milk and the usual food return once rehydrated, juice and fizzy drinks wait until the diarrhea stops, and a child at higher risk gets 5 mL/kg of ORS after each large watery stool. No antidiarrheal drugs and no routine antibiotics. Vomiting usually lasts 1 or 2 days and stops within 3 days in most; diarrhea usually lasts 5 to 7 days and stops within 2 weeks. Parents come back if the child looks more unwell, becomes irritable or lethargic, passes less urine, or has pale or mottled skin or cold hands and feet.

IV rehydration: isotonic fluid for the deficit plus maintenance, electrolytes and glucose checked at the start and regularly, potassium added once the level is known, ORS restarted early, and the IV stopped once ORS is tolerated. Hypernatremic dehydration is corrected slowly, over about 48 hours, with expert advice.

nodes.ask: Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2 weeks to 3 months. Imaging?
options: Ultrasound of the pylorus, with electrolytes and a venous gas
Upper GI contrast series as the first study, for the string sign
A plain film to look for a caterpillar-shaped stomach
CT of the abdomen with oral contrast to show the pyloric channel
nodes.chainStep: Abdominal ultrasound of the pylorus (muscle thickness, channel length, and whether gastric contents pass); electrolytes with chloride and potassium, a venous gas and glucose; the surgeon told once it is confirmed
nodes.why: Ultrasound is usually appropriate as the first study for new non-bilious vomiting from 2 weeks to 3 months (ACR) and is highly accurate: it shows a constant, thick-walled, elongated pylorus with no passage of gastric content. The upper GI series can show the beak or string sign but is less ideal first when pyloric stenosis is likely, and radiographs are most often not helpful. CT is not among the studies ACR rates for it. The classic chemistry is a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, now present in under half because the diagnosis comes earlier.

orders.dose: StatPearls: wall 3 mm or more and channel 15 mm or more. ACR: muscle 4 mm or more with length over 18 mm, though 3 to 4 mm may be positive in a premature or younger neonate
orders.note: The two sources set different cut points; ACR adds that pylorospasm and evolving pyloric stenosis overlap.

orders.dose: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; now found in less than half

outcomes.if: Pyloric stenosis; thick, long pylorus, no gastric emptying
Pylorus normal; measurements normal, contents pass

nodes.ask: Pyloric stenosis on ultrasound, alkalosis on the gas. Next?
options: IV fluid with saline, dextrose and potassium; operate once corrected
Pyloromyotomy tonight, with the electrolytes corrected under anesthesia
Smaller, thickened feeds by mouth; surgery if the vomiting persists
IV 0.9% saline, holding the potassium until after the surgery
nodes.chainStep: Consider a nasogastric tube; IV rehydration with potassium chloride (StatPearls: 5% dextrose with 0.25% saline and 2 mEq KCl per 100 mL if mildly dry, more saline if moderately or severely dry); electrolytes and gas rechecked; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis is corrected (a 2026 trial: chloride over 100 and bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L)
nodes.why: Pyloric stenosis is not truly urgent: the infant is rehydrated and the electrolytes corrected first, and then the pyloromyotomy follows. StatPearls corrects and follows the bicarbonate because of the risk of hypoventilation, and it is generally assumed that the alkalosis should be corrected before surgery to prevent apnea. Potassium goes in with the fluid. Feeds do not relieve an obstruction whose treatment is surgical, and saline alone leaves the hypokalemia.

orders.dose: StatPearls: 5% dextrose with 0.25% saline and 2 mEq KCl per 100 mL if no or mild dehydration, higher saline concentrations if moderate or severe. 2026 trial: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline boluses set by the chloride and bicarbonate, plus 1.5 times maintenance; its control arm, 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline at 1.25 to 2 times maintenance, potassium by urine output. NICE NG29: isotonic maintenance fluid, and 0.9% saline with potassium for ongoing losses
orders.note: Hypotonic or isotonic, steady or bolus correction: the sources share no regimen.

orders.dose: Chloride over 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L and base excess near normal (2026 trial)
orders.note: A 2020 systematic review found the concentrations needed before pyloromyotomy unknown; one series aimed at chloride 90 or more.

orders.dose: Consider one

nodes.summary: Pyloric stenosis: rehydration and electrolyte correction first, then a pyloromyotomy, open or laparoscopic, which is curative with very low morbidity. Feeding starts 4 to 8 hours after recovery from anesthesia; up to 80% have some milder vomiting afterwards, and vomiting that persists 5 days after surgery earns an upper GI series.

options: Surgeon now; nasogastric tube, IV fluid and an upper GI series
Contrast enema first, to find out where the cecum lies
Ultrasound, with malrotation excluded if the SMA and SMV look normal
An ORS trial with ondansetron, imaging if the vomiting goes on
nodes.chainStep: Urgent surgical review; nasogastric or orogastric decompression, IV fluid, broad-spectrum antibiotics; upper GI contrast series in a stable infant (ultrasound may show the whirlpool sign of volvulus); peritonitis, sepsis or instability goes to theatre without waiting for imaging
nodes.why: Green vomit is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and volvulus can progress to necrosis within hours, so the surgeon is involved at once and the stomach decompressed. For bilious vomiting after the first 2 days of life ACR rates the upper GI series usually appropriate; it is the reference standard, although false negatives occur. Ultrasound may be appropriate, and its whirlpool sign is specific for volvulus, but a normal SMA and SMV relationship does not preclude malrotation. A contrast enema is not a first study (up to 15% have a normal mobile cecum), and treating green vomit as gastroenteritis misses the emergency.

orders.dose: Airway protection, nasogastric or orogastric decompression, IV fluid, broad-spectrum antibiotics, urgent surgical consultation
Peritonitis, sepsis or instability: the operating room, often without waiting for complete imaging
ACR 2020: upper GI series usually appropriate, ultrasound may be appropriate. StatPearls 2026: ultrasound has become the preferred first study for bilious vomiting in neonates

sources.where: Evaluation: ultrasonography; Evaluation: upper GI series

orders.note: The sources disagree on the first test; both keep the upper GI series as the reference standard in a stable infant.

orders.dose: Not stated in the sources read

outcomes.if: Malrotation, with or without volvulus; DJ flexure right of the spine, corkscrew
Normal rotation; DJ flexure left of the spine at the pylorus

nodes.summary: Malrotation: surgery. With volvulus it is an emergency: the bowel is untwisted counterclockwise and a Ladd procedure done, with an appendectomy; with advanced ischemia the volvulus is simply reduced and a second-look laparotomy follows 24 to 36 hours later, and necrotic bowel is resected conservatively. In a stable child, a high index of suspicion still prompts early operation when volvulus is likely.

Normal rotation on the upper GI series. The study is the reference standard but not perfect (96% sensitive in one review), so a high suspicion still keeps the surgeon involved; an equivocal series goes on to a small bowel follow-through to the cecum. Other causes of bilious vomiting, such as atresia, Hirschsprung disease and lower obstruction, are not covered in this version.

nodes.ask: Colicky attacks with pallor in a child under 3. Next?
options: Abdominal ultrasound, bedside or formal; a film only for free air
Plain abdominal films to make the diagnosis before ultrasound
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to confirm it
A diagnostic contrast enema as the first study, before ultrasound
nodes.chainStep: Abdominal ultrasound (point-of-care or radiology) for the target sign; IV access and fluid; an abdominal film only to look for free air or obstruction; the surgeon aware
nodes.why: Ultrasound is the first-line test, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 94 to 97%, and point-of-care and radiology scans perform alike (ACR); it shows the target sign and can find a lead point or another diagnosis. A 2-view film is only 62% sensitive and serves to exclude perforation or obstruction. CT is not first-line given the performance of ultrasound, and a contrast enema is now kept for a nondiagnostic ultrasound or for treatment. The classic picture of pain, vomiting, bloody stool and a mass is seen in only about 20%, so the diagnosis rests on the scan.

orders.dose: 3 to 36 months; the classic pain, vomiting, bloody stool and mass in only about 20%
Target or doughnut sign on the transverse view, pseudokidney on the longitudinal; high negative predictive value

nodes.label: Ultrasound, with a film if needed

outcomes.if: Ileocolic intussusception, stable; target sign, no peritonitis or free air
Intussusception with peritonitis, free air or shock; on scan and film
No ileocolic intussusception; none seen, or a short small bowel one

nodes.ask: Ileocolic intussusception, stable, no peritonitis. Next?
options: Image-guided air or contrast enema reduction, with the surgeon aware
Laparotomy and manual reduction as the first-line treatment here
IV antibiotics first, then the enema reduction once they have run in
Admit and repeat the ultrasound in 6 hours, as many reduce by themselves
nodes.chainStep: Fluoroscopic or ultrasound-guided air or liquid enema reduction (air pressure up to 120 mmHg); IV access; surgeon available; no pre-reduction antibiotics
nodes.why: Nonoperative enema reduction is the treatment of choice unless there are signs of perforation or peritonitis, with a pooled success of 82%; pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy is the most widely used. APSA found prophylactic antibiotics do not decrease complications and are unnecessary. Spontaneous reduction belongs to transient small bowel intussusception, not the ileocolic kind, and surgery is for failure, perforation, peritonitis or shock.

orders.dose: Upper limit 120 mmHg
Unnecessary: they do not decrease post-reduction complications
Pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis or shock: surgery instead
About 0.4% of enemas; tension pneumoperitoneum gets emergent midline supraumbilical paracentesis, then immediate surgery
Multiple recurrences are not a contraindication to enema reduction

sources.where: Enema reduction; Outcomes; Small bowel intussusception; Conclusion

outcomes.if: Reduced; mass gone, air or contrast floods the small bowel
Partly reduced, stable; mass moved back, no peritonitis
Not reducible, or perforated; no progress, or free air

nodes.summary: Reduced intussusception: the child can be observed in the ED and discharged (APSA), with parents taught to return if the symptoms come back. It recurs in about 9 to 15% after enema reduction, half within the first few days, more often after age 1; APSA counsels the parents of children over 2 about a slightly higher risk. A recurrence is reduced by enema again, and repeated recurrences raise the chance of a pathological lead point.

Partly reduced and stable: a delayed repeat enema, for a medically stable child without peritonitis. About half of those whose first enema fails then reduce and avoid surgery; the interval is not standardized, commonly 15 minutes to a few hours. If it still fails, surgery follows, with a laparoscopic approach considered first.

Surgery: peritonitis, free air or shock rule out an enema, and an irreducible intussusception or a perforation during the enema goes to theatre. APSA considers a laparoscopic approach first, for a shorter stay with similar complications; if the surgeon cannot reduce it, the segment is removed.

No ileocolic intussusception on a good ultrasound. When none is seen, its negative predictive value of 99.7% rules intussusception out at this visit, and the scan may show another diagnosis. A short small bowel intussusception found on ultrasound is usually transient and reduces on its own.

nodes.ask: Right lower quadrant pain, then vomiting. Next?
options: Score it (PAS or pARC) with a blood count and CRP; image if not low
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast as the first imaging test
Make the diagnosis from the PAS and book the appendectomy
Rule it out if the white count and neutrophils are both normal
nodes.chainStep: Pediatric Appendicitis Score (cough, percussion or hopping tenderness 2; right lower quadrant tenderness 2; anorexia, fever, nausea or vomiting, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, migration of pain 1 each) or the pARC; blood count with neutrophils and CRP; early surgical consultation
nodes.why: WSES recommends routine blood tests and inflammatory markers in a child with suspected appendicitis, combining them with scores to decide on imaging, but advises against diagnosing it on scores alone; the PAS and Alvarado score are useful for excluding it. A normal white count does not exclude appendicitis. CT is not routine first-line imaging in children, where ultrasound comes first.

orders.dose: 10 points: cough, percussion or hopping tenderness 2; right lower quadrant tenderness 2; anorexia, pyrexia, nausea or emesis, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, migration of pain 1 each
Staged pathway (ACR, citing Saucier): 4 to 7 is the equivocal band sent to ultrasound. Dutch review: 5 or less rules it out. StatPearls: 6 or more suggests appendicitis
orders.note: Each source draws the PAS cut points differently; this pathway images every PAS of 4 or more, as ACR's intermediate band does.

orders.dose: Under 5% very low, 5 to 14% low, 15 to 84% intermediate, 85% or more high; validated at 5 to 20.9 years
In the derivation paper, not read (its copy is blocked), so it is not computed here
CRP 10 mg/L or more and a white count of 16,000 or more are strong predictors in children

outcomes.if: Below the equivocal band; PAS 3 or less
Equivocal or higher; PAS 4 or more

options: Right lower quadrant ultrasound, with the surgeon involved early
CT with and without IV contrast, to stage it before ultrasound
Pelvic ultrasound instead, since a low appendix lies in the pelvis
A plain abdominal film to look for an appendicolith
nodes.chainStep: Graded ultrasound of the right lower quadrant (point-of-care first where expert); a noncompressible appendix over 6 mm with wall thickening is diagnostic; if equivocal or nondiagnostic with suspicion persisting, MRI (preferred over CT in children) or CT with IV contrast
nodes.why: Ultrasound is the preferred first imaging in children (StatPearls, WSES) and usually appropriate at intermediate risk (ACR); WSES rates point-of-care ultrasound first-line in adults and children. At high clinical risk, ACR notes that some go straight to surgery and others image first, rating right lower quadrant ultrasound, MRI without contrast or CT with IV contrast as may be appropriate. ACR rates pelvic ultrasound and CT without and with IV contrast usually not appropriate at both intermediate and high risk; it rates the plain film usually not appropriate at high risk, and its panel disagreed on it at intermediate risk.

orders.dose: A noncompressible, enlarged appendix over 6 mm with wall thickening
CT with IV contrast, MRI without contrast, or MRI without and with contrast are each usually appropriate (ACR); WSES prefers MRI over CT as second line in children

sources.where: Summary of highlights; Variant 2 and 3 rating tables

outcomes.if: Appendicitis; noncompressible appendix over 6 mm
No appendicitis seen; normal appendix, or not seen

nodes.summary: Appendicitis in a child: surgery. pw_abdominal_pain carries the adult management; its antibiotic doses are adult doses, and a child's agent and dose are not in this pathway's sources. WSES does not delay surgery beyond 24 hours for uncomplicated appendicitis in a child and operates within 8 hours for complicated appendicitis. Nonoperative treatment is for carefully selected children only (StatPearls criteria include age over 7, symptoms under 48 hours, no appendicolith and an appendix under 1.1 cm).

Appendicitis not shown. A low-risk child is not imaged (ACR), and a negative or inconclusive ultrasound does not reliably exclude appendicitis (StatPearls). With suspicion persisting, ACR goes on to MRI or CT with IV contrast; watchful waiting can be considered when the appendix was not seen.

nodes.ask: Bloody diarrhea in a vomiting child. Next?
options: Stool toxin and culture now, with a blood count, film and creatinine
CT of the abdomen with contrast for colitis before the stool tests
Loperamide with the ORS to slow the losses until the culture is back
No stool tests, as diarrhea in children rarely needs a culture
nodes.chainStep: Stool for Shiga toxin and culture; blood count with film for schistocytes, metabolic panel with creatinine, LDH and haptoglobin; no antimotility drugs; antibiotics are a source conflict (WHO 2024 gives them for blood in the stool, the STEC sources avoid them); specialist advice on monitoring for HUS if STEC is found
nodes.why: Blood or mucus in the stool is an indication for stool microbiology (NICE), and a stool for Shiga toxin goes with any diarrhea in a possible HUS. Antibiotics, above all beta-lactams, and antimotility drugs are avoided in STEC because they are linked to HUS and worse outcomes; NICE keeps antibiotics for specific infections such as dysenteric shigellosis. WHO 2024 recommends antibiotics for every child up to 10 with blood in the stool, so the sources conflict. The stool tests come first (NICE), and none of the sources read images the bowel for bloody diarrhea. Skipping the culture is right only for non-bloody diarrhea.

orders.dose: Microbiology with blood or mucus in the stool; Shiga toxin whenever diarrhea is present in a possible HUS
Specialist advice on monitoring for HUS

orders.item: Antibiotics for blood in the stool
orders.dose: WHO 2024: antibiotics for every child up to 10 years with blood in the stool, first line ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days. StatPearls: generally avoided while STEC is possible; beta-lactams relatively contraindicated
orders.note: WHO treats bloody diarrhea as shigellosis; the STEC sources withhold antibiotics because they are linked to HUS; NICE gives them for specific infections such as dysenteric shigellosis.

orders.dose: Loperamide and similar agents raise the risk of systemic complications
HUS begins 5 to 13 days after the diarrhea starts (median 6.5 to 7 days), most often under 5 years
Blood count with differential, metabolic panel, LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin and a smear for schistocytes; ADAMTS13 to rule out TTP

outcomes.if: HUS; anemia with schistocytes, low platelets, kidney injury
No HUS yet; count, film and creatinine normal

nodes.summary: STEC-associated HUS: supportive care with careful volume repletion (too little volume is linked to more renal replacement therapy, which half need), red cells as needed, platelets sparingly, and no antibiotics or antimotility drugs; nephrology early. ADAMTS13 is sent to rule out TTP, and the rash pathway (pw_rash) carries the same HUS route.

Bloody diarrhea, no HUS yet: rehydration as for gastroenteritis, no antimotility drugs, and antibiotics withheld once STEC is found (StatPearls; WHO 2024 gives them for any blood in the stool), and specialist advice on monitoring for HUS when STEC is found, since HUS begins 5 to 13 days after the diarrhea starts. If the stool grows another pathogen, NICE gives antibiotics for specific infections such as dysenteric shigellosis.
